diagrams.name: anat-p235-occlusal-elevations
diagrams.title: Occlusal anatomy and height of contour

diagrams.name: anat-p236-anterior-landmarks
diagrams.title: Anterior tooth landmarks and height of contour

cloze.text: In the TMJ, the {{c1::mandibular condyle}} is the rounded part of the mandible that fits into the {{c2::temporal}} bone to form the joint.
The TMJ {{c1::articular disc}} is a {{c2::fibrocartilaginous}} pad that cushions the joint and divides it into {{c3::upper and lower compartments}}.
The {{c1::mandibular fossa}} is the depression in the {{c2::temporal}} bone where the mandibular condyle sits.
The TMJ {{c1::joint capsule}} is a fibrous enclosure around the joint that contains {{c2::synovial fluid}}.
In the TMJ, {{c1::synovial fluid}} lubricates the joint and provides {{c2::nutrients}}.
The TMJ {{c1::ligaments}} support the joint and limit {{c2::excessive joint movement}}.
The {{c1::articular eminence}} is a bony ridge on the temporal bone just {{c2::in front of (anterior to)}} the mandibular fossa; it guides the condyle and disc during {{c3::jaw opening}}.
TMJ locking (lockjaw) happens when the {{c1::mandibular condyle}} gets stuck, preventing the jaw from opening or closing properly.
cloze.extra: It occurs in two main ways: open lock and closed lock.

cloze.text: TMJ open lock: the condyle moves {{c1::too far forward}} and gets stuck {{c2::in front of the articular eminence}}, so the patient {{c3::can't close}} the mouth.
cloze.extra: Can happen after wide opening during yawning or dental treatment.

cloze.text: TMJ open lock can happen after {{c1::wide opening}}, e.g. during yawning or dental treatment.
TMJ closed lock: the condyle {{c1::can't move forward}} properly, often due to {{c2::disc displacement}}, so the patient {{c3::can't open the mouth fully}} (limited opening).
The {{c1::anatomic crown}} is the part of the tooth covered by {{c2::enamel}}, coronal to the {{c3::cementoenamel junction (CEJ)}}.
The CEJ is a key landmark for {{c1::probing depth}}, {{c2::attachment loss}}, and {{c3::restoration margins}}.
The {{c1::clinical crown}} is any part of the tooth {{c2::visible in the mouth}}.
{{c1::Crown lengthening}} procedures increase the clinical crown for better restoration attachment.
A long clinical crown can signal {{c1::gingival recession}} or {{c2::periodontal disease}}.
{{c1::Coronal}} = direction toward the {{c2::crown}}.
The {{c1::anatomic root}} is the part of the tooth covered by {{c2::cementum}}, located {{c3::apical}} to the CEJ.
cloze.extra: Book misprints "coronal to the CEJ" — the anatomic root is apical to the CEJ.

cloze.text: The {{c1::clinical root}} is the part of the root covered by the {{c2::gingiva}}; not visible in the mouth.
The {{c1::apex}} is the tip or end of the root.
The {{c1::periapex}} is the area surrounding the root tip (apex).
The {{c1::apical foramen}} is the opening at the root tip through which {{c2::nerves and blood vessels}} enter.
{{c1::Apical}} = direction toward the {{c2::apex of the root}}.
The {{c1::furcation}} is the area where roots divide in {{c2::multi-rooted}} teeth; site for possible bone loss ({{c3::furcation defect}}).
The {{c1::roof of the furcation}} is the 'ceiling' of the furcation, closest to the crown.
The {{c1::root trunk}} is the section of the root from the {{c2::CEJ}} to the {{c3::furcation}} (where roots begin to divide).
{{c1::Root concavities}} are depressions on the {{c2::mesial and/or distal}} root surfaces (e.g. maxillary 1st premolars and mandibular molars).
Root concavities are prone to {{c1::plaque retention}}, making them higher risk for {{c2::periodontitis}} and {{c3::root caries}}.
Roots tend to tilt {{c1::distally}} ({{c2::inclination}}) or may be curved ({{c3::dilaceration}}).
Furcations only occur in {{c1::multi-rooted}} teeth.
Maxillary molars have {{c1::3}} roots → {{c2::3}} furcations: {{c3::buccal, mesial, distal}}.
Mandibular molars have {{c1::2}} roots → {{c2::2}} furcations: {{c3::buccal and lingual}}.
The periodontium includes the {{c1::cementum}}, {{c2::alveolar bone}}, {{c3::gingiva}}, and {{c4::periodontal fibers}} surrounding the tooth.
Enamel is the {{c1::hardest}} structure in the body, {{c2::96%}} mineralized.
Enamel is {{c1::non-living}} tissue and contains {{c2::no nerves}}.
Enamel is mineralized by apatite crystals containing {{c1::calcium}} and {{c2::phosphate}} (known as {{c3::hydroxyapatite}}).
Enamel is hardest at the {{c1::biting edges or cusps}}.
The enamel of primary teeth is {{c1::softer}} and {{c2::thinner}} than that of permanent teeth.
Dentin is {{c1::70%}} mineralized and functions to {{c2::protect the pulp}}.
The {{c1::bulk of the crown}} is composed of dentin, but dentin is also present in the {{c2::root}}.
Coronal dentin is covered by {{c1::enamel}}; root dentin is covered by {{c2::cementum}}.
Cementum is approximately {{c1::50%}} mineralized — {{c2::less}} than dentin.
cloze.extra: That's why you shouldn't put too much pressure on root surfaces when scaling.

cloze.text: Because cementum is less mineralized than dentin, avoid putting {{c1::too much pressure on root surfaces}} when scaling.
Mineralization ranking: enamel {{c1::96%}} > dentin {{c2::70%}} > cementum {{c3::50%}}.
The {{c1::pulp}} is the innermost part of the tooth; it contains the {{c2::nerves}}, {{c3::blood vessels}}, and {{c4::lymphatics}}.
Incisors function to bite and {{c1::cut}} food.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Incisor → scissor → cut; Canine → dog → dogs love tearing clothes and shoes; Mole (Mexican sauce of ground ingredients) → molar → grind.

cloze.text: Canines (cuspids — {{c1::one}} cusp) function to pierce or {{c2::tear}} food.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Incisor → scissor → cut; Canine → dog → dogs love tearing clothes and shoes; Mole (Mexican sauce of ground ingredients) → molar → grind.

cloze.text: Premolars (bicuspids — {{c1::two}} cusps) assist {{c2::molars}} in grinding and assist {{c3::canines}} in piercing and tearing.
Molars function to {{c1::grind}} food, assisted by premolars.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Incisor → scissor → cut; Canine → dog → dogs love tearing clothes and shoes; Mole (Mexican sauce of ground ingredients) → molar → grind.

cloze.text: The {{c1::facial}} surface faces the face; called "{{c2::labial}}" for anteriors and "{{c3::buccal}}" for posteriors.
The {{c1::lingual}} surface faces the tongue; also called "{{c2::palatal}}" for maxillary teeth.
{{c1::Mesial}} = towards the midline; {{c2::distal}} = away from the midline.
{{c1::Incisal}} = biting surface of {{c2::anterior}} teeth; {{c3::occlusal}} = chewing surface of posterior teeth.
The {{c1::contact area}} is the area that touches the adjacent tooth in the same arch.
An open contact between adjacent teeth in the same arch is known as a {{c1::diastema}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know? Diastemas can result from labial frenum attachment, tongue thrusting, missing teeth, or tooth-to-jaw size discrepancy.

cloze.text: Diastemas can result from {{c1::labial frenum attachment}}, {{c2::tongue thrusting}}, {{c3::missing teeth}}, or {{c4::discrepancy in tooth-to-jaw size}}.
The {{c1::interproximal space}} is the area between adjacent teeth.
A {{c1::cusp}} is a rounded elevation on the {{c2::occlusal}} surface.
The {{c1::cingulum}} is a rounded elevation (convexity) on the {{c2::lingual}} surface at the {{c3::cervical third}} (near CEJ) of {{c4::anterior}} teeth.
A major {{c1::lingual fossa}} is noticeable below (incisal to) the cingulum.
All anterior teeth form from {{c1::four}} centers of development (lobes): {{c2::three facial}} and {{c3::one lingual}}.
The {{c1::lingual}} lobe of an anterior tooth becomes the {{c2::cingulum}}.
{{c1::Maxillary}} anterior teeth have a larger, well-developed cingulum; {{c2::mandibular}} anteriors have a smoother, rounded cingulum.
The {{c1::height of contour}} is the greatest {{c2::bulge}} or convexity on the crown of a tooth.
On the buccal and lingual surfaces, the height of contour prevents {{c1::food from accumulating}} on the tooth and protects the {{c2::gingiva}}.
On the mesial and distal surfaces, the height of contour is the {{c1::contact area}} between adjacent teeth.
A {{c1::ridge}} is a {{c2::linear, flat}} elevation on teeth (e.g. buccal ridge, mesiolingual ridge).
On anterior teeth, marginal ridges are on the mesial and distal borders of the {{c1::lingual}} surface; on posterior teeth, on the mesial and distal borders of the {{c2::occlusal}} surface.
{{c1::Triangular ridges}} project from the {{c2::cusp tips}} to the {{c3::central groove}}.
cloze.extra: They are "inside" the occlusal surface, vs. the marginal ridges on the mesial and distal borders.

cloze.text: Each triangular ridge forms "half" of an {{c1::oblique}} ridge or half of a {{c2::transverse}} ridge.
{{c1::Transverse ridges}} are formed by the union of two {{c2::triangular ridges}} on posterior teeth meeting on a {{c3::faciolingual}} line.
{{c1::Oblique ridges}} are found on the occlusal surface of {{c2::maxillary molars}}, formed by the union of two triangular ridges.
An oblique ridge extends from the {{c1::mesiolingual}} cusp to the {{c2::distobuccal}} cusp.
A {{c1::groove}} is a narrow linear depression on the occlusal surface.
{{c1::Supplemental grooves}} are secondary grooves derived from the {{c2::primary (developmental)}} grooves on occlusal surfaces.
A {{c1::fossa}} is a depression on a tooth surface.
{{c1::Lingual fossae}} are shallow depressions on the lingual surfaces of {{c2::anterior}} teeth.
A lingual fossa may contain a {{c1::lingual pit}}, most commonly seen on {{c2::maxillary lateral incisors}}.
The {{c1::central fossa}} is a deep depression in the central portion of the {{c2::occlusal}} surfaces of posterior teeth.
A {{c1::pit}} is a small pinpoint depression at the junction of {{c2::developmental grooves}}; it facilitates {{c3::biofilm retention}}.
Pits are commonly present on the {{c1::buccal}} surface of the {{c2::mandibular first molar}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Brad Pitt → buccal pit → be aware of the buccal pits on molars.

cloze.text: {{c1::Buccal pit}}: depression on the buccal aspect of the tooth. {{c2::Central pit}}: depression on the occlusal surface.
A {{c1::fissure}} is a deep cleft between adjoining {{c2::cusps}} on posterior teeth.

mcq.question: Which nerve innervates the muscles of mastication?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: CN V3 = motor to mastication. The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) is the only branch with motor fibers; it innervates all four muscles of mastication.

mcq.question: Which artery supplies the mandibular teeth?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Inferior alveolar = mandibular teeth. The inferior alveolar artery enters the mandibular foramen and supplies all lower teeth.

mcq.question: Which landmark is located just behind the maxillary third molar?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Maxillary tuberosity = posterior to maxillary molars. The maxillary tuberosity is a rounded elevation distal to the last upper molar.

mcq.question: Which papillae provide texture sensation but do not contain taste buds?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Filiform = tactile only. Filiform papillae are the most numerous and aid in mechanical function, not taste.

mcq.question: Which movement occurs first during mouth opening?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: TMJ rotation = first phase. Opening begins with rotation of the condyle in the lower joint space, followed by anterior translation.

mcq.question: Which structure is at risk of puncture during a PSA nerve block?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: PSA block = hematoma risk. The pterygoid plexus is close to the maxillary tuberosity and can be injured during injection.

mcq.question: Which artery supplies the lips and muscles of facial expression?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Facial artery = lips and face. The facial artery crosses the mandible to supply superficial facial structures.

mcq.question: Which lymph nodes drain the mandibular incisors?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Submental = chin, lower lip, incisors. The submental nodes sit under the chin and drain the anterior floor of mouth and lower anterior teeth.

mcq.question: Which tongue muscle is responsible for protrusion?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Genioglossus = stick tongue out. The genioglossus originates from the genial tubercles and moves the tongue forward.

mcq.question: Which cranial bone houses the mandibular fossa involved in TMJ function?
mcq.explanation: Keywords: Temporal bone = mandibular fossa. The mandibular condyle sits in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone to form the TMJ.
